#167149. Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3342 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.
  • Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated.
  • The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.

Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

Industry observers note that in the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

“It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn swiftly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Sources indicate that miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký.

According to recent reports, during totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

According to recent reports, druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

According to recent reports, an image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly highlights Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

He photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

In a recent development, he insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”.

A composite sequence of photographs shows the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Václav Široký and Miloslav Druckmüller.

Recent findings suggest that despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

Industry observers note that on the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

The corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

Sources indicate that to observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most important processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

That’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

According to recent reports, space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very swiftly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography.

According to recent reports, the European Proba-3 mission, debuted in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

Sources indicate that when Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

It has been revealed that it took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

Habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”.

The error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” indicates Habbal.

It has been revealed that capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.).

In a recent development, the human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

To create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller states. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

According to recent reports, since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

The teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

In a recent development, but duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

“Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller says wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

In a recent development, if you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký.

Industry observers note that on the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller says with a grin. “It’s perfect.”.

But even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” says Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

Recent findings suggest that as the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

It has been revealed that twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký.

Sources indicate that those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

According to recent reports, around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

In a recent development, “That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller indicates with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

The optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek.

“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” says Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”.

For example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

With just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Recent findings suggest that druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as quickly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

It has been revealed that “The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller notes. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”.

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký.

It has been revealed that but for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller notes.

It has been revealed that who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

#167148. ‘Odyssey’ Cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema Was More Interested in the Intimate Than the Epic

‘Odyssey’ Cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema Was More Interested in the Intimate Than the Epic

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1140 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that christopher Nolan‘s adaptation of Homer’s “The Odyssey” was one of the most awe-inspiring cinematic achievements of 2026, an epic worthy of comparison with the grandiose visions of David Lean and Stanley Kubrick.
  • “We never really treated it in an epic way,” van Hoytema told IndieWire.
  • Given that, van Hoytema tried not to be seduced by the beauty of his surroundings if it didn’t serve the emotional experience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that christopher Nolan‘s adaptation of Homer’s “The Odyssey” was one of the most awe-inspiring cinematic achievements of 2026, an epic worthy of comparison with the grandiose visions of David Lean and Stanley Kubrick. Yet what interested cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema was less the story’s vast scale than the details of the human faces inhabiting the film‘s sweeping vistas.

“We never really treated it in an epic way,” van Hoytema told IndieWire. “Even though we all know ‘The Odyssey‘ and understand the scale of the story, making some sort of a tourist film was never on our agenda. It was the characters and the visceral sense of their experience that we were interested in, so even standing in the most crazy places in the world — on mountaintops or wherever — we were never motivated by the landscapes. The settings take care of creating the scale and scope of the film — our perspective on the story was a very intimate one.” Related Stories Forget Photorealism: How ‘Wildwood’ Made Its Handmade Digital Artistry Visible ‘Cliff Booth’ Brings Back a Fan-Favorite ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood’ Face.

Given that, van Hoytema tried not to be seduced by the beauty of his surroundings if it didn’t serve the emotional experience. “It was less about showing how beautiful a beach was than about showing how shitty those men felt when they were on the beach,” he remarked, noting that a key tool in getting across the characters’ internal feelings was shooting the film entirely in IMAX.

“Shooting an entire film in IMAX has been a pursuit of ours for quite a long time now, and we’ve been tweaking the lenses and tweaking the cameras in order to get there,” van Hoytema noted. “We’ve managed to wrangle the equipment and technology around it to enable us to be right there next to you, looking straight into your eyes.”.

This again plays into that idea of intimacy versus scale, which was something van Hoytema and Nolan had experimented with in “Oppenheimer.” In that film, IMAX was used not only for major set pieces like the atomic bomb test, but quiet dialogue scenes shot largely in close-up. Van Hoytema says that he and Nolan have long been aware that IMAX has historically been used mostly to depict the wonders of the world, but they wanted to expand its grammar.

According to recent reports, “The lenses that we use today are an evolution of different iterations of lenses that we have been building through the years, lenses that focus extremely close and that can open wide so that you can work with natural light or in half-darkness,” van Hoytema mentioned. “We’ve found that IMAX is an intimate format because it’s such a good replicator of the human experience and perspective.”.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest obstacle toward shooting an entire movie in IMAX before “The Odyssey” was always the sound — IMAX film cameras are famously noisy, making it difficult to get decent production recordings. “We built a blimp on ‘Tenet,’ but it didn’t work,” van Hoytema said. “This was the first film where we felt that the technology had gotten far enough to actually shoot the entire thing on IMAX. There’s been an evolution in development not only in my department but in the sound department — they have come up with better microphones, better filtration, and in this film it came together beautifully.”.

Van Hoytema and Nolan always had a backup plan in case the IMAX cameras became too unwieldy or got in the way of performance, particularly in lengthy dialogue scenes that would outlast the cameras’ short magazines. Once Matt Damon and Anne Hathaway proved that they could pull off a complicated sequence in close collaboration with van Hoytema and the other departments, however, Nolan and his crew were confident they could rely on IMAX as their format of choice. “That day was the hardest, and we shot everything on IMAX, so for the rest of the film we just committed — no plan B,” van Hoytema stated.

According to recent reports, while van Hoytema and Nolan were enthusiastic about committing to IMAX, it did create massive logistical challenges — not just when it came to getting the heavy camera and blimp in and out of remote locations, but in terms of performance. The actors’ eyelines, for example, were often blocked by the enormous camera. “Here we are bragging about the intimacy we can achieve, and suddenly you’re on set with a gigantic black box in front of the actors, and they can’t look each other in the eyes,” van Hoytema stated. “It was a huge problem.”.

It has been revealed that to solve the problem, van Hoytema and his crew built a system that would allow the actors to see each other. “It was based on a teleprompter that has an angled mirror in front of the lens, and people can look straight into the lens reading a teleprompter because it has projected text on it. But instead of text, we had another mirror, and we had an actor sitting here. So basically what actors see is a little surface with a mirror with the other actor in there, and they can look straight into the other actor’s eye.”.

Van Hoytema could fine-tune the eyelines by adjusting the angles of the mirrors in what he called “a very analog but very effective solution. And the actors loved it, because instead of looking at a wall they’re literally looking at their co-stars.” Van Hoytema reiterated the idea that everything in the movie was geared toward character and performance — including, at times, making the actors as uncomfortable as possible.

In a recent development, “It’s not for nothing that Chris loves to go out at sea with a ship and do things that are almost physically impossible,” van Hoytema said. “The more miserable or real or wet the situation is, the more the actors have to react to and play with. And that also goes for my way of working. I love different weather situations. I love different light situations. I love kinetic and physical challenges. It adds something unexpected and something visceral. The camera’s always fighting something and the actors are fighting at that very same moment, so it becomes a weirdly symbiotic relationship to the elements.”.

In spite — or perhaps because — of the arduous shoot, van Hoytema didn’t want to see it end. “This was an extremely difficult film, but it was also the film where everything we’d been working toward came together,” van Hoytema. “We were much more light-footed. Weirdly enough, when what you’re doing becomes subjected to elements that you cannot control, you become a bit less precious. And that lack of preciousness is very liberating. We just went in headfirst.”.

The new book has offered more insight into why George Lucas’ original plans for the Star Wars sequel trilogy never made it to the substantial screen. Although Disney bought Lucasfilm in 2012, Iger reportedly ensured that Disney was under no legal obligation to follow through on every project or idea the company had.

Industry observers note that in a recent interview on The Town podcast, Whelan discussed the complicated relationship between Disney and the Star Wars franchise. The journalist spoke about what were reportedly Lucas’ original storylines for the sequel trilogy movies, as well as Iger’s alleged reaction to them and creative decisions.

Whelan’s book claims that Iger wanted to purchase Lucas’ massive franchise but also ensure that the acquisition agreement did not require the studio to use his ideas, as he reportedly did not like the creator's ideas. A source who was involved in the negotiations claimed that Iger disliked the original storylines so much that he had no intention of adapting them at all.

Belloni: Lucas actually had treatments for three Star Wars movies that he wanted Disney to make after the acquisition. You write this in the book: ‘After reading the plot outlines, Iger decided Disney had to buy them, but he made sure to write into the contract that Disney had no legal obligation to actually make the movies. Another person who was involved in the negotiation recalls that Iger hated the treatments and said privately, ‘We are not making these movies, How bad were they?

Industry observers note that whelan: Imagine you’re an executive who’s never written a movie, never directed a movie, and George Lucas sends you a package of scripts, and you look at these and say, ‘This is terrible. We’re never making this.’.

So, instead of going with Lucas' undisclosed plans, Disney ultimately went in a upcoming direction. The industry giant launched its sequel trilogy with 2015’s Star Wars: The Force Awakens. Directed by J.J. Abrams, the film became a massive commercial success, earning over $2 billion at the box office worldwide.

However, despite the success of Disney's first Star Wars film, the next two installments were less well-received. Rian Johnson’s Star Wars: The Last Jedi got overall positive reviews from critics, but fans weren't entirely happy with it. Abrams’ Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker received more mixed reviews across the board. Both movies also earned less at the box office than the first film.

While it is impossible to know how Lucas’ sequel trilogy would have performed, Whelan’s claims provide more context surrounding Disney’s creative decisions involving Star Wars. It should also be noted that neither Disney nor Iger have confirmed the allegations in The House of Mouse: Bob Iger and the War of Succession at Disney, so anything written in the book should be taken with a grain of salt and not as fact.

  • According to recent reports, for decades, sovereign wealth funds were among private equity's most deep-pocketed backers, entrusting billions of dollars to buyout firms to invest on their behalf.
  • From originating transactions and taking controlling stakes in companies to building their own investment platforms, some of the world's largest state investors are adopting the playbook of traditional private equity giants, according to industry veterans.
  • "The imminent change is that the lines between LPs and GPs are becoming increasingly blurry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, for decades, sovereign wealth funds were among private equity's most deep-pocketed backers, entrusting billions of dollars to buyout firms to invest on their behalf. Increasingly, they are doing the dealmaking themselves.

From originating transactions and taking controlling stakes in companies to building their own investment platforms, some of the world's largest state investors are adopting the playbook of traditional private equity giants, according to industry veterans.

"The imminent change is that the lines between LPs and GPs are becoming increasingly blurry. This could bring more fundamental changes in the long term," Diego Lopez of Global SWF told CNBC.

Limited partners, or LPs, typically commit capital to private equity funds, while general partners, or GPs, are responsible for sourcing deals and managing investments.

Sovereign funds and state investment companies are increasingly taking on the GP role, Lopez stated, pointing to the establishment of their own private equity management platforms, such as Mubadala Capital and Singapore's Seviora.

The shift is also reflected in the way some of the world's largest sovereign investors are approaching dealmaking.

"They originate transactions rather than waiting for them. They build platforms rather than buying single assets. They take control positions and operate what they own," PwC stated in their latest report on sovereign wealth funds.

"Whether you're a company, a general partner, or a government, you'll find that these institutions are no longer the limited partner you're raising money from; they're the principal sitting across the table.".

Last year, Abu Dhabi's MGX, an investment vehicle established by state fund Mubadala in 2024, anchored the roughly $40 billion acquisition of Aligned Data Centers alongside BlackRock, Nvidia and Microsoft. A year earlier, a consortium led by Mubadala Capital acquired a 68% equity stake in alternative asset manager Fortress, which at the time managed more than $48 billion.

Some sovereign funds are striking deals at a speed typically associated with large private equity firms, according to PwC.

Singapore's GIC recorded 553 transactions between July 2023 and July 2026, Abu Dhabi's Mubadala 397 and the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority 367, according to PwC's analysis of PitchBook data, which includes transactions by subsidiaries.

It has been revealed that the shift comes as sovereign wealth funds command unprecedented financial firepower. Their assets have surged about 59% over the past five years to $16.5 trillion, up from $10.4 trillion in 2022 and more than nine times the $1.8 trillion they managed in 2005, according to data provided to CNBC by research firm Global SWF which focuses on state-owned investors.

PwC projects that sovereign wealth fund assets to reach $22.4 trillion by 2030.

While sovereign funds' push into direct investing has been underway for years, a more challenging fundraising environment for PE firms and a resurgence in megadeals have recently accelerated the trend.

The fundraising slowdown has tilted bargaining power toward large institutional investors, allowing them to negotiate more opportunities to invest directly alongside private equity managers, said Kyle Walters of PitchBook.

Industry observers note that A key attraction is the potential to save on fees. Co-investments typically carry little or no management fees and no carried interest, which is the share of investment profits that managers receive. Additionally, direct deals can eliminate external manager fees altogether.

"For a large SWF writing substantial checks, the fee savings in dollar terms can be substantial," Walters said.

Recent findings suggest that sovereign funds also enjoy structural advantages over traditional buyout firms. Unlike conventional private equity funds, which operate within predetermined lifespans, sovereign investors can hold assets for decades, the experts highlighted.

They can also deploy substantial sums from their own balance sheets without having to raise fresh capital, an advantage particularly valuable in capital-intensive sectors such as AI infrastructure and energy.

But deep pockets and patient capital alone do not guarantee success.

As sovereign wealth funds take controlling stakes in companies, they assume operational responsibilities traditionally borne by private equity managers, while potentially stretching their own capacity to source deals, conduct due diligence and manage complex assets, PwC cautioned.

"Building the required capability, the talent, the systems, and the governance is a slower process than committing the capital," PwC said. The firm also flagged concentration risks as sovereign investors increasingly pile into similar investment themes, particularly AI, data centers and power infrastructure, leaving even geographically diversified portfolios vulnerable to the same underlying risks.

Despite their growing ambitions, industry experts are skeptical that sovereign wealth funds will supplant established private equity managers.

"This newly introduced path these large LPs are paving is more of a partnership than a competition between GPs and LPs," Walters stated, noting that much of the increased activity is taking the form of co-investments.

He pointed to the $55 billion take-private deal for video-game maker Electronic Arts declared last year, in which Saudi Arabia's PIF contributed significant capital, as an example of how both sides ae joining hands.

Traditional buyout firms also retain an edge in sourcing deals and managing portfolio companies.

"However, capital alone does not replace the specialist sourcing, operational expertise, and active ownership capabilities required to consistently create value, which experienced managers have built over time," said Vincent Ng, managing director and co-head of Asia at Partners Group.

Direct investing also raises concentration risks, while illiquidity could become a problem during crises when governments need access to capital, experts noted.

Rather than displacing traditional buyout firms, sovereign investors' growing ambitions could change the economics of private equity, forcing managers to become more flexible in how they work with their biggest clients.

"This is likely to reshape the relationship between asset owners and managers, with more customized mandates, co-investments, and long-term partnerships," Ng remarked.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two decades ago, comedy was one of the reliable genres when it came to box office hits. The likes of Jim Carrey's Bruce Almighty, 2009's The Hangover, and the comedy sequel Meet the Fockers all made roughly $500 million at the box office, and the future looked bright for Hollywood's funniest faces. However, in the past 16 years, the comedy genre's share of the theatrical market has dropped from 20% to 10%, and production companies are losing faith in pure comedy, instead choosing to weave their humor through other genres, such as horror.

For the first time in 16 years, a once bankable comedy franchise is venturing into an entirely upcoming box office landscape with its long-awaited fourth installment. This week, Focker-in-Law, the fourth film in the Fockers franchise, hopes to challenge the likes of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping at the Thanksgiving box office. The franchise began with the 2000 rom-com Meet the Parents, and a lot has changed since.

That is, except for the main cast, with Robert De Niro, Ben Stiller, Owen Wilson, and Teri Polo all returning for this fourth installment. The biggest new addition to the franchise is Wicked star and Academy Award nominee Ariana Grande, who plays the trained FBI hostage negotiator girlfriend of Greg's son Henry (Skyler Gisondo), as she is quickly welcomed into the Circle of Trust, much to Greg's dismay. Blythe Danner and Beanie Feldstein also feature in the film, which is written and directed by John Hamburg, based on a story by Hamburg, Ilana Glazer, and Austen Earl.

According to recent reports, we've already reported that Focker-In-Law has been met with a terrible batch of first reviews, earning just 31% on review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes. Collider's Gabrielle Moss awarded the film just 5/10 in her review, saying that "Stiller and Grande never generate the joyful friction that Stiller and DeNiro produced in the original film." However, fans of the franchise have been pleasantly surprised, scoring 87% on Rotten Tomatoes, with this fairly glowing response helping the film earn a positive CinemaScore, which is officially a "B+.".

Industry observers note that focker-In-Law is now in theaters. For all the latest movie news, make sure to stay tuned to Collider.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Star Trek: Discovery introduced the best First Officer replacement for Captain Saru (Doug Jones), but audiences only got one season with him because Paramount+ canceled the series. Star Trek: Discovery premiered in 2017, and its success sparked multiple upcoming Star Trek series and a streaming movie executive produced by Alex Kurtzman and Secret Hideout. However, Paramount+ ended the series with season 5 in 2024.

Industry observers note that the USS Discovery was unique in several ways, starting with its spore displacement hub drive allowing it to jump to a new location instantaneously. Discovery's bridge, however, saw a game of musical chairs, with multiple Starfleet Officers (and a couple pretending to be) taking command of the starship before Captain Michael Burnham (Sonequa Martin-Green) became Disco's permanent master at the end of season 3.

Naturally, the USS Discovery's captaincy in flux meant the First Officer would be, as well. Michael Burnham, Saru (Doug Jones), and even Lieutenant Sylvia Tilly (Mary Wiseman) took turns as Discovery's Number One. Saru surprisingly served as Burnham's XO while also holding the rank of Captain. Star Trek: Discovery season 5 ended this turnover with a fantastic replacement for Saru who only lasted that lone season.

In a recent development, star Trek: Discovery season 5 introduced Commander Rayner (Callum Keith Rennie), the best replacement First Officer the series produced. The former Captain of the USS Antares, Rayner was a Kellerun who had a distinguished 30-year Starfleet career before he was forced into retirement for his extreme methods in hunting down Moll (Eve Harlow) and L'ak (Elias Toufexis).

Sources indicate that surprisingly, Captain Burnham personally requested Rayner as her upcoming First Officer despite their animosity. Rayner accepted a demotion to Commander and became Burnham's Number One, and that's when the magic happened. Gruff, no-nonsense, and not keen on the USS Discovery crew's overly-familial culture, Rayner was the ideal foil for the passionate and action-oriented Captain Burnham.

Rayner was also a stark contrast to Saru, who became a Federation Ambassador and married T'Rina (Tara Rosling), the President of Ni'Var. Burnham and Saru shared a close-knit bond, but Rayner challenged Michael and kept Discovery's crew on business differently than Saru. In Star Trek: Discovery's series finale, Rayner becomes acting Captain, finally taking the center seat, and leads the saucer-separated USS Discovery to defeat the Breen.

Sadly, Star Trek: Discovery fans only enjoyed a brief 10 episodes with Commander Rayner and the formidable presence of Callum Keith Rennie. The Canadian actor who memorably played the Cylon Leoben Conroy brought some of the welcome grit of Battlestar Galactica into Star Trek: Discovery. Rayner emerged as a fan favorite, but his story was cut short when it was just getting started.

Star Trek: Discovery was expected to run for seven seasons, just as the series set in Star Trek: The Next Generation's 24th century did under executive producer Rick Berman. Discovery wrapped production on season 5, and showrunner Michelle Paradise hadn't yet begun to map out season 6 when Paramount+ delivered an unexpected axe to Disco.

Star Trek: Picard ended in 2023 after its planned three seasons, but Paramount+ ignored fan outcry and never put its proposed spinoff, Star Trek: Legacy, into development.

In 2023, Skydance Media began purchasing Paramount Global, which was completed in 2025. The rapid expansion of Paramount+'s Star Trek franchise under executive producer Alex Kurtzman suddenly stopped, and the streamer began canceling its existing Star Trek series. Star Trek: Discovery was the second show Paramount+ ended after it canceled and purged all episodes of Star Trek: Prodigy from its service.

It has been revealed that star Trek: Discovery's fifth and final season premiered on Paramount+ in March 2024 and was over in late May. Star Trek: Lower Decks ended with season 5 in December of that year. Star Trek: Strange Latest Worlds ultimately received five seasons, ending in 2027, while the newest series, Star Trek: Starfleet Academy, only got two seasons before it also ends in 2027. With that, the decade-long Kurtzman era that began with Star Trek: Discovery comes to a close.

While small fry in terms of the massive picture of Star Trek's streaming era, Commander Rayner was an unfortunate casualty of corporate acquisitions and mergers. Star Trek: Discovery was intended to go on to season 6 and continue Commander Rayner's story, likely to culminate in a seventh and final season. In a better timeline, that's what happened.

Star Trek: Discovery is streaming on Paramount+.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones are the most recent entry in Sony's 1000X series, which has been around since 2016. They're the best over-ear headphones in terms of audio quality presently on the market—but not everyone can (or needs to) drop nearly half a grand on headphones.

Recent findings suggest that the WH-1000XM5 are a generation older and were at the top of their class until they were supplanted by the XM6. On the plus side, by virtue of being older, they're at the moment discounted to $198 (down from the original $399.99) during Amazon's early Black Friday sale. That 50% off brings it down to the lowest price they've ever reached, a good deal for premium headphones that still sound incredible, even in 2026.

I have been a loyal customer of the 1000X line for many years; they're my go-to headphones for most activities. The WH-1000XM5 received an "outstanding" review from PCMag for their top-notch audio quality and exceptional audio when using the best-in-class active noise cancellation. The headphones are also well-designed to be comfortable for long listening sessions. The ear controls use tapping and swiping, which isn't my favorite, but it's what all modern headphones are moving toward. There's a companion app that lets you adjust your EQ settings to your liking, including what the swiping and tapping functions do.

These headphones also have a stereo 3.5mm connection, which is perfect for those who want to use a cable and not worry about battery life. And speaking of battery life, Sony states you can expect about 30 hours, but it will vary depending on your use of ANC. #167123. How Do You Land on a Moon With Almost No Gravity?

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2971 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

How Do You Land on a Moon With Almost No Gravity?

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2971 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Japan’s MMX mission aims to sample the Martian moon Phobos.
  • Japan's MMX spacecraft will fire its engines to slow down and enter orbit around Mars.
  • Last August, looking up from the edge of an ancient river delta on Mars, the Perseverance rover’s electronic eye spied an oblong shadow crossing the distant, glowing Sun.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Japan’s MMX mission aims to sample the Martian moon Phobos.

Japan's MMX spacecraft will fire its engines to slow down and enter orbit around Mars.

Last August, looking up from the edge of an ancient river delta on Mars, the Perseverance rover’s electronic eye spied an oblong shadow crossing the distant, glowing Sun. Phobos, the Martian moon named for the Greek god of fear and panic, was transiting the solar disk. Too small to darken the pale, dust-tinged sky, but orbiting close enough to eclipse a significant fraction of the Sun, Phobos passed in less than a minute.

NASA’s Perseverance rover captured Phobos passing in front of the Sun from the surface of Mars.ASU/MSSS/SSI/JPL-Caltech/NASA.

The tiny moon, with its murky origins, is an enigma, and one whose makeup and history could tell us much about Mars and the wider solar system. And now the international Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission, which successfully launched on 20 October, seeks to explore that mystery with an unprecedented series of landings on the unknown surface of Phobos.

In a recent development, this mission brings unusual challenges—for example, designing an orbit to study a microgravity moon orbiting a much larger planet. Engineers also had to figure out how to assess and land on this low-gravity pile of loosely assembled dirt and rock, how a rover might rove across it, and how the spacecraft might take samples and return them to Earth.

“I often say that landing on Phobos is like trying to land a balloon,” notes Yasuhiro Kawakatsu, project manager of MMX at the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). “It’s very difficult to drop a balloon to the ground and prevent it from tilting or bouncing.”.

Industry observers note that phobos is one of two small Martian moons; the other is Deimos, named after the Greek god of dread and terror. Their cosmic origins are unknown, though there are two prevailing theories. One holds that the moons were once asteroids from the belt between Mars and Jupiter, captured by the smaller planet’s gravity. In the other theory, Phobos and Deimos formed when a large celestial body slammed into Mars, sending debris into orbit. Some models suggest the pair are the last survivors from a cluster of satellites.

The enormous Stickney crater, roughly 9 kilometers across, dominates this view of Phobos taken by NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.University of Arizona/JPL-Caltech/NASA.

Scientifically speaking, Phobos is considered a rubble pile, a loosely consolidated aggregate of rock and dust. Far too small to become spherical under its own mass, it’s shaped like a lumpy potato, roughly 27 kilometers in length, with only 1/1,800th of Earth’s gravity. On Phobos, a typical adult would weigh about as much as a tennis ball does on Earth.

Recent findings suggest that more than 10 years in the making, MMX launched on Japan’s flagship H3 rocket from Tanegashima spaceport on 20 October local time. It will arrive at Mars in 2027 carrying scientific payloads from several space agencies, including NASA, and a new rover called Idefix developed by the French and German space agencies (CNES and DLR) in collaboration with JAXA.

Engineers assembled MMX’s modules at Japan’s Tanegashima Space Center before the spacecraft’s October 2026 launch.JAXA.

Industry observers note that MMX consists of three modules: a propulsion module to power its journey to Mars and apply the brakes to enter orbit around the red planet; an exploration module carrying the rover, sampling gear, and other scientific instruments; and a return module, attached to the exploration module, that harbors the capsule destined for a high-speed reentry into Earth’s atmosphere. After collecting samples on Phobos, the exploration and return modules will lift off together. The exploration module will then be jettisoned while the return module sets a course back home.

In a recent development, if all goes according to plan, MMX will deliver a 10-gram sample to Earth in the second half of 2031. But the mission will face a series of daunting challenges to reach that end point, including navigating complex orbits around Phobos and landing on its surface while Mars periodically blocks communications with Earth.

The MMX’s modular design includes the propulsion module [left] and the exploration and return modules [right].Kyodo News/Getty Images.

“It’s the most complex mission I have ever seen,” says Patrick Michel, director of research at CNRS (the French National Center for Scientific Research) and co-principal investigator on Idefix.

An H3 rocket carried MMX into space on 20 October 2026, beginning the mission’s five-year journey to Phobos and back.The Asahi Shimbun/Getty Images.

Industry observers note that once MMX reached low Earth orbit, its propulsion module’s engine fired, kicking off a nearly year-long deep-space cruise to Mars. On arrival, the spacecraft will need to fire its engines in an extended, carefully timed burn to slow down enough to be captured by Mars gravity. The propulsion module will then be jettisoned, leaving the exploration and return modules to orbit Mars.

“If something doesn’t go according to plan, MMX will fly by Mars and get catapulted into the solar system,” indicates Nicola Baresi, an astrodynamicist who coauthored a paper on specially designed orbits for MMX.

In a recent development, from that initial orbit, MMX will transition into a specially designed quasi-satellite orbit that allows it to keep pace with the small moon but also move around it. Since Phobos is too small to orbit in the conventional sense, the spacecraft will orbit Mars alongside the moon, following a clever egg-shaped path that slings MMX alternately ahead of and behind the moon. “When you’re closer to Mars, you’re accelerating with respect to Phobos, and when you’re farther from Mars, you’re decelerating. So you essentially go back and forth,” explains Baresi.

Martian Maneuvers To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.Chris Philpot.

To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.

In a recent development, the best existing images of Phobos, from spacecraft such as NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and ESA’s Mars Express, have resolutions of only a few meters per pixel. That’s larger than Idefix, the mission’s rover, itself about the size of a microwave oven. To map the surface in greater detail, MMX will loop in front of and behind Phobos at distances ranging from 200 kilometers to less than 20 km from the surface.

In a recent development, during its two-year remote sensing campaign, the exploration module will use several cameras and a laser altimeter to map the surface in high resolution and look for candidate landing sites. When Mars passes behind the Sun as seen from the Earth, causing a roughly two-week communications blackout, MMX will retreat into a larger, stable orbit. After communications resume, MMX will prepare to send its first visitor down to the surface.

It has been revealed that before the exploration and connected return modules attempt to land, Kawakatsu notes, MMX will send a scout that in Japanese is called “the first penguin,” leaping into unknown waters. For this mission, the first to leap will be the Idefix rover, named for the canine companion to Obelix in the French comics series Asterix. The exploration module will release the rover during a low-altitude pass of between 40 and 100 meters above Phobos’s surface in 2028 or early 2029.

MMX will use its TENGOO camera [left] and LIDAR laser altimeter [right] to map Phobos’s terrain.JAXA.

It will be a tense moment that calls back to 2005, during Japan’s Hayabusa mission to explore the asteroid Itokawa. In a similarly designed drop, the MINERVA rover was released from an orbiter, but erroneously at 200 meters instead of the intended 70 meters. The rover missed the asteroid and, without propulsion, drifted off into deep space.

Sources indicate that idefix will get a slight nudge out of the exploration module toward its negligible-gravity target, freefalling and likely tumbling as it goes. It’s expected to touch down with a velocity of less than 1 meter per second. Unlike rovers that have landed on other surfaces with airbags or dedicated landing legs, Idefix will land without protection, apart from some extra padding on the solar panels due to their critical nature. The barely-there gravity of Phobos should allow the 23-kilogram rover to land softly, though exactly how this landing will play out is hard to predict.

The Idefix rover will travel to Phobos with its wheels tucked in and solar panels folded.DLR.

Recent findings suggest that “It will bounce probably several times,” states Stephan Ulamec, Idefix’s co-principal investigator and project manager at DLR. “It will come to rest somehow in some position.” Once it’s still, four retracted legs will deploy to right the rover autonomously, regardless of its orientation. It will then unfold its solar panels to charge its batteries for exploration tasks ahead.

A simulation shows how Idefix is expected to tumble onto Phobos, right itself using its articulated legs, and begin exploring the moon’s surface. DLR.

Industry observers note that once operational, Idefix will roll at a snail’s pace, topping out at one millimeter per second. Its metal wheels have protruding blades like a paddle wheel, designed to gain traction in Phobos’s microgravity. “If we were to drive our rover faster, then it would actually be more like we were swimming through instead of driving across the surface,” notes Cecily Sunday, a doctoral student involved in testing Idefix’s WheelCams at the Institut Superieur de l’Aeronautique et de l’Espace (ISAE-Supaéro) in Toulouse, France.

The WheelCams, a pair of cameras placed on the underside of the rover, will observe the wheels and their tracks during Idefix’s planned 100-Earth-day primary mission. The images will help researchers study the size and distribution of grains in Phobos’s regolith and how cohesive they are. How much or how little the grains stick together will greatly impact how Idefix moves. Sunday likens this to the difference between driving on dry and wet sand. “Think of trying to build a sandcastle with dry sand,” she notes. “You can’t. Add water, and suddenly you can.”.

The Idefix rover was mounted between the MMX spacecraft’s landing legs for the journey to Phobos.DLR.

Industry observers note that the team tested the rover’s nine-bladed wheels on a variety of materials, including Phobos regolith simulants provided by JAXA and DLR, lunar simulants, glass beads, quartz sand, and clay pebbles. “We characterize the mechanical properties of each simulant precisely, then test across the full range, with varying grain size, angularity, and even color, so we can map what we see in the WheelCam images back to actual surface properties,” Sunday indicates.

Recent findings suggest that despite the microgravity and Phobos’s rubble-pile nature, Sunday says Earth-based tests can approximate the rover’s motion on the surface of the small moon fairly well. While Phobos’s reduced gravity lowers the rover’s effective weight, there is also reduced pressure between the grains beneath its wheels. “As long as you’re moving very, very slowly and using the same materials and the same weight of the system, they should be representative,” Sunday says.

With four paddle-like wheels and deployable solar panels, Idefix is designed to crawl across Phobos.Ardan Fuessmann/Imago/Alamy.

Idefix’s interactions with its upcoming home will offer “sub-millimeter resolution and information on porosity, on grain size, on surface strength, on how hard is the material,” Ulamec says. “It fills a gap between remote observations from orbit and detailed observations of the return samples back on Earth.”.

What Idefix finds on this rocky, rugged world will help determine how and where JAXA attempts to land the main spacecraft. Michel indicates the touchdown will provide ground truth for understanding of Phobos. When NASA’s OSIRIS-REx spacecraft touched down on the asteroid Bennu to collect a sample, its sampling arm surprisingly sank nearly half a meter into the loose material. But Ulamec doesn’t think Idefix will sink deep into Phobos, noting that Bennu is very different and much smaller, with a diameter of 500 meters.

Once Idefix has investigated the surface, MMX will face an even greater challenge: landing its much larger exploration module on Phobos. The spacecraft will make a controlled descent to roughly 10 meters above the surface, then drop the remaining distance in free fall. With so little gravity to pull it downward, even a small sideways motion could cause the lander to tip or bounce away. A successful, upright landing would mark the start of up to two hours on Phobos for the crucial sampling phase.

The MMX mission draws on the experience and technologies of Japan’s two Hayabusa sample-return missions, which landed on the asteroids Itokawa and Ryugu. But this mission has many more moving parts. MMX’s exploration module will use two sampling devices—a coring sampler developed by JAXA and a pneumatic sampler provided by NASA and fabricated by Honeybee Robotics, a subsidiary of Blue Origin. Data from these tools, and those carried by the Idefix rover, could answer questions about the origin of Phobos and how the Mars system has evolved.

Sources indicate that the coring sampler uses a robot arm and a cylindrical corer designed to reach at least 2 centimeters below the surface. The arm can maneuver to find the best site for digging. “That by itself is a challenge because we’ve never done it,” Michel indicates. “You never know what can happen at the very sampling site itself, where you might have a boulder and the arm cannot move.”.

Industry observers note that probing beneath the top layer will be valuable because solar radiation, galactic cosmic rays, and micrometeorites have battered and weathered the surface. The material below should offer a better record of the moon’s origins, and JAXA aims to collect at least 10 grams of it.

MMX will carry both the Idefix rover [bottom] and a robotic coring sampler [top] designed to dig beneath Phobos’s weathered surface.JAXA.

The pneumatic sampler takes a different approach. Mounted on one of the lander’s legs, it will inject pure, non-reactive nitrogen gas into the surface and capture the grains stirred up. This sample could illuminate the changes Mars and its moons have undergone over time. The dual system also adds redundancy in the face of Phobos’s unknowns. “If the surface of Phobos proves to be very hard, [the coring sampler] may struggle to penetrate the ground. [The pneumatic sampler] would not experience this issue and still be able to gather material,” Kawakatsu says.

One of the most intriguing aspects of MMX is the additional possibility of collecting material from the planet below. It’s likely that Phobos has been peppered by Martian ejecta thrown into space by meteor impacts, so MMX also provides an opportunity to return the first Martian samples to Earth. Michel estimates that the samples could contain “a few hundred grains coming from Mars.” Scientists can distinguish those grains from native Phobos material by analyzing their oxygen isotopes.

Recent findings suggest that that possibility raises a planetary-protection question. A direct Mars sample-return mission would have to follow strict rules to ensure that potentially living biological material from Mars doesn’t contaminate Earth. But those protocols don’t apply to MMX, even if its sample does collect grains of Martian soil. A panel of experts concluded that any microbes blasted off Mars wouldn’t survive the violent impact and ejection or the intense radiation exposure on the way to Phobos. This saved MMX from implementing expensive and time-consuming quarantine and containment protocols for the returning sample.

After landing on Phobos, MMX will have roughly two hours to collect samples from the moon’s surface before lifting off again.JAXA.

During the brief surface operation, the robotic arm will deposit the samples in a storage unit, from which they’ll be transferred into a capsule aboard the return module and sealed in a vacuum. After that, lift off.

According to recent reports, once back in Mars orbit, the exploration module will resume its observations of Phobos and make several flybys of Mars’s other diminutive moon, Deimos, to gather data on its surface, structure, and composition. In November 2030, during a favorable alignment of Mars and Earth, MMX will begin the homeward leg of its trip. The return module will separate from the exploration module and power the voyage home, its sole objective to bring the dust of Phobos to Earth.

MMX’s sample return capsule will carry material from Phobos through Earth’s atmosphere in 2031.JAXA.

Finally, in 2031, the 60-centimeter-wide sample capsule will plunge into Earth’s atmosphere at roughly 12 kilometers per second. Assuming it survives the extreme heat of reentry and lands safely in Australia, scientists will begin to tease out clues about Phobos and the early solar system. JAXA’s Institute of Space and Astronautical Science will receive and curate the samples, which will also be shared with mission partners.

It has been revealed that “We have macroscale measurements from the spacecraft, microscale measurements with the rover, and then sample analysis,” Michel claims. “So we can relate the three kinds of scales together because we have all of them.” The insights gleaned from orbital images, close-up images of the regolith, and the chemical analysis of the samples could have wider implications for our understanding of our solar system.

It has been revealed that “MMX is a mission to understand the Mars system and shed light onto how terrestrial planets like the Earth, and maybe Mars, develop a habitable environment,” Kawakatsu states. “We strongly suspect that our terrestrial planet region formed dry, and water and organics were scattered inwards from the icy-rich outer solar system.” Mars, he says, sits at the gateway between the inner and outer solar system, making its moons valuable witnesses to the processes that shaped potentially habitable worlds.

HBO’s 6-Part Miniseries Is Still One of the Best Ever Made

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, molly DeCastro is a Newly introduced York-based emerging film and entertainment journalist with a personal passion for poetic prose and impactful storytelling.
  • Recent findings suggest that I Know This Much Is True, adapted from Wally Lamb’s 1998 bestselling novel, follows the fractured yet mirrored lives of identical twin brothers.
  • In short, the audience meets the Birdsey brothers at a sore spot in their lives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, molly DeCastro is a Newly introduced York-based emerging film and entertainment journalist with a personal passion for poetic prose and impactful storytelling. She graduated from Pace University with a degree in English and a concentration in creative writing. While film analysis is at the heart of her work, she is especially interested in exploring cinema through an anthropological lens and in examining how creative themes reflect cultural identity. She aims to forge a deep connection between audiences and film through thoughtful and evocative writing. She also enjoys keeping up with all things film! That means specializing in industry news, emerging directors, and stand-out projects.

Recent findings suggest that I Know This Much Is True, adapted from Wally Lamb’s 1998 bestselling novel, follows the fractured yet mirrored lives of identical twin brothers. Starring Mark Ruffalo as both Dominik and Thomas Birdsey, the story centers on the aftermath of crisis and the relentless passage of time and age. Their bond, despite its strain, somehow captures the inescapable weight of generational trauma and the confusing yet undying devotion found between brothers. Director Derek Cianfrance paints a beautiful, tragic story, showing with immense care and depth the tenderness of the human experience.

In short, the audience meets the Birdsey brothers at a sore spot in their lives. Thomas, a lifelong paranoid schizophrenic, in a very public and violent fashion, protests the Gulf War by sacrificing his own hand. Consequently, he’s thrust into the legal system with only his brother Dominik on the outside to vouch for him. All at once, he must go from being a brother to the sole advocate and protector, all the while unearthing his own trauma as his story unfolds.

Sources indicate that ruffalo's claim to fame is, of course, tied to Marvel. Because of this, it can be easy to forget what a truly stellar performer he is. Critics and fans alike have pointed to his performance of Thomas and Dominik Birdsey as the most emotionally raw and resonant of his entire career. Each character demands something entirely different. Each is incredibly complex, nuanced, and requires an incredible level of adaptability and grace to pull off. Ruffalo appears to balance both Thomas's schizophrenia and Dominik’s grief effortlessly.

According to recent reports, while scenes with himself are incredible, so are scenes with his cast mates. Alongside Kathryn Hahn as Dessa, Dominik's ex-wife, or Rosie O'Donnell as Thomas's social worker, sometimes clashing with them in these significant, loud, cross-cutting conflicts or sharing these quiet, near-whispered intimate moments, with such a high level of skill captured on screen, there is so much room for play and for depth. Much of the series is heavy, some have said, exhaustively so. However, the performances tugging it along are most certainly worth a watch.

As is often the case when a series comes from a book, the plot of this show is truly incredible. The care and poignancy are evident from the very beginning. The Bridsey brothers were born into a family with many, many dark secrets. Each of them bears the weight. Their mother is a submissive, exploited woman, controlled by their abusive stepfather. He had a particular affinity for abusing Thomas as well, claiming he was soft and often asking for punishment. Notably, for the sake of their protection, she never revealed their birth father’s identity.

Present day, decades later, Dominic is a bit shifty but relatively stable in comparison to Thomas, who developed schizophrenia and fell in and out of institutions for years. Through creating a past so tight and intricately woven, their present becomes all the more deep. Each of their motives becomes entirely intuitive to the audience, and thus one not only feels for the Birdsey boys, but feels deeply connected to them. As the story progresses, the desperation grows thicker. Things unravel rather promptly. Dominik is unrelenting in his pursuit to vindicate his brother, and Thomas is entirely reliant on his persistence. The flashbacks and winding plots within the series are both truly sickening and incredibly loving. That combination makes for a truly thrilling experience.

The series achieved both commercial and critical success. Ruffalo won an Emmy, as well as a Golden Globe, and a Screen Actors Guild Award. It holds a highly decorated 74% on Rotten Tomatoes, and by all accounts is an incredible must-watch. There are very few series that result in unanimous approval, and This Much I Know Is True earned exactly that. From the plot to the performances to the original novel itself, each piece of the puzzle created a highly decorated, well-loved masterwork.

Following the parallel lives of identical twin brothers Dominick and Thomas Birdsey in a story of betrayal, sacrifice, and forgiveness.

#167120. Breaking: 10 Spies More Lethal Than James Bond
